summary: Amisulpride is a substituted-benzamide atypical antipsychotic used for acute and chronic schizophrenia; low doses (50-300 mg/day) target predominantly negative symptoms while higher doses (400-800 mg/day, up to 1200 mg/day) treat predominantly positive/acute symptoms. It is largely eliminated unchanged by the kidneys, so dose reduction is required in renal impairment, whereas hepatic adjustment is rarely needed. It strongly raises prolactin and causes dose-dependent QT prolongation; it is approved in Europe (EMA/UK SPC, BNF) but the oral form is NOT FDA-approved in the US.
indications: Acute and chronic schizophrenia with predominantly positive symptoms (higher doses)
Schizophrenia with predominantly negative symptoms (lower doses)
Mixed positive and negative symptom presentations

Doses above 300 mg/day should be given in two divided doses
May be taken with or without food

moa: Selectively binds dopamine D2 and D3 receptors with no appreciable affinity for serotonergic, histaminergic, cholinergic, or adrenergic receptors. At low doses it preferentially blocks presynaptic D2/D3 autoreceptors, enhancing dopaminergic transmission and improving negative symptoms; at higher doses it blocks postsynaptic limbic dopamine receptors, reducing positive (psychotic) symptoms. Limbic selectivity over striatum contributes to a relatively lower extrapyramidal burden, but D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway markedly elevates prolactin.

absolute: Concomitant prolactin-dependent tumours (e.g., pituitary prolactinoma, breast cancer)
Children before the onset of puberty
relative: Elderly with dementia-related psychosis (increased mortality and stroke - antipsychotic class effect)
Known QT prolongation, bradycardia, congenital long QT, or family history of QT prolongation
Risk factors for stroke or VTE

preg: Not recommended during pregnancy unless clearly necessary; amisulpride crosses the placenta. Neonates exposed during the third trimester are at risk of extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia or hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, respiratory distress, feeding disorder) varying in severity and duration. Monitor exposed neonates accordingly.
lact: Amisulpride is excreted into breast milk in relatively large amounts. Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment; a careful risk-benefit assessment is required.
renal: Amisulpride is eliminated largely unchanged in the urine, so dose reduction is required in renal impairment: reduce to half the dose if creatinine clearance is 30-60 mL/min, and to one-third if CrCl is 10-30 mL/min. There is no experience below 10 mL/min - use with particular care. Consider intermittent treatment courses in severe impairment.
hepatic: Amisulpride is only weakly metabolised by the liver, so a dosage reduction is generally not necessary in hepatic impairment.

major: Class IA antiarrhythmics e.g. quinidine, disopyramide (additive QT - contraindicated/avoid)
Class III antiarrhythmics e.g. amiodarone, sotalol (additive QT - contraindicated/avoid)
Other QT-prolonging drugs (e.g. methadone, some antipsychotics, certain antimalarials, IV erythromycin)
moderate: Drugs causing hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia (diuretics, stimulant laxatives, amphotericin B) - correct before use
Other CNS depressants and sedatives (additive sedation)
interactions.food: No clinically significant food effect; may be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; additive CNS depression and sedation
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum prolactin (can interfere with prolactin-based diagnostics and pregnancy/fertility tests); may prolong the ECG QT interval

common: Extrapyramidal symptoms - tremor, rigidity, hypokinesia, hypersalivation, akathisia
Hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, gynaecomastia, breast pain, erectile dysfunction)
emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, raised CPK)
Torsades de pointes / serious ventricular arrhythmia

monitoring: Baseline and periodic ECG (QT interval), especially with dose increases or added QT-prolonging drugs
Serum electrolytes - potassium and magnesium (correct before and during treatment)
Renal function (creatinine clearance) to guide dosing
Prolactin level if symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia
Metabolic parameters: weight/BMI, fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipids
Extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia
Signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, altered consciousness)
counsel: May cause drowsiness - take care with driving or operating machinery
Report palpitations, fainting, or irregular heartbeat (possible QT effect)
Report breast swelling/discharge, menstrual changes, or sexual dysfunction (raised prolactin)
Report fever with muscle stiffness or confusion urgently (neuroleptic malignant syndrome)
Do not stop abruptly; discuss any dose changes with your prescriber
Tell your clinician about pregnancy, breastfeeding, kidney problems, and all other medicines
pk: Antipsychotic effect over days to weeks; sedation earlier
Two plasma peaks: ~1 hour and ~3-4 hours after an oral dose
Supports once- or twice-daily dosing depending on total dose
Store below 25-30 degrees C; protect from moisture; keep in original packaging
pearls: Oral amisulpride is NOT FDA-approved (approved in Europe per EMA/UK SPC and used per BNF); pending clinical review. The IV antiemetic Barhemsys is a separate FDA-approved product for PONV, not the antipsychotic indication.
Dose-dependent dual mechanism: low doses (50-300 mg/day) for negative symptoms via presynaptic autoreceptor block; high doses (400-800 mg/day, up to 1200) for positive symptoms.
Largely renally cleared and weakly metabolised - renal function, not hepatic function, drives dosing decisions.
Among the antipsychotics most likely to raise prolactin; counsel on and watch for hyperprolactinaemia.
Causes dose-dependent QT prolongation - obtain ECG, correct K+/Mg2+, and avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs.
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the usual schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up. Keep dosing times consistent.
overdose: Experience is limited; effects exaggerate the pharmacology - sedation, hypotension, extrapyramidal symptoms, and potentially serious cardiac effects including dose-dependent QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. There is no specific antidote. Manage with supportive measures, continuous cardiac/ECG monitoring of vital functions, correction of electrolytes, and anticholinergic agents for severe extrapyramidal symptoms. Amisulpride is poorly dialysed.
refs: FDA - Barhemsys (IV amisulpride for PONV; separate product, not oral antipsychotic)
